tool_summary: Sends a signal to all processes matching a given name. Unlike pkill's pattern matching, killall typically requires an exact name match, which somewhat narrows accidental over-matching, but by design still targets every instance of that name.
platform_notes: killall exists on both GNU/Linux (psmisc) and macOS/BSD, but the two implementations differ meaningfully: GNU killall matches by process name substring/exact-match with several qualifier flags, while macOS/BSD killall's argument handling and available flags differ. This ruleset covers the common baseline (bare invocation and -9); flag-specific rules should be revisited if platform divergence proves significant in practice.

rules.description: On some BSD/macOS killall implementations, invoking killall with no name argument at all signals every process the caller has permission to signal, rather than erroring -- a fundamentally different and far more dangerous behavior than GNU killall's exact-name-match requirement. Since platform cannot be reliably determined from the command string alone, this is treated as the worst case.
rules.notes: GNU killall requires a name argument and will error without one, so this rule is a false positive on Linux. Given the severity asymmetry (a blocked benign Linux invocation vs. an unflagged system-wide signal broadcast on BSD/macOS), erring toward ERROR here is intentional.

rules.description: SIGKILL (-9 or -KILL) terminates all matched processes immediately without allowing them to clean up, flush buffers, or release resources gracefully.

Sends a signal (SIGTERM by default) to every currently running process matching the given name. Affects all instances of that process name at once, not a single targeted PID. Severity here is WARNING rather than INFO because killall's exact matching behavior (substring vs. exact name, and available flags) genuinely differs between GNU/Linux and macOS/BSD (see platform_notes, llm_confidence: medium); this is platform-behavioral uncertainty, not CLI drift over time.
